A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SynFlowNet research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material across moves and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original molecule-generation benchmarks, backward-policy and scaling ablations, and target-specific computational case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds SynFlowNet results for rediscovery, KRAS docking, additional optimization tasks, vocabulary-controlled novelty, and sample efficiency.

M1.justification: The reaction-based action space, graph-transformer policies, fingerprint-based selection, objectives in Equations 1–3, and Algorithms 1–2 are retained. Expanded reaction-encoding and docking-reward documentation does not establish a change to the underlying generation procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds aripiprazole and celecoxib rediscovery, KRAS docking optimization, and JNK3 optimization. It also trains on building blocks extracted from ChEMBL molecules, whereas v2 used ChEMBL as a novelty reference. These extend task requirements, target coverage, and the represented training vocabulary.

E2.justification: SynNet becomes an evaluated comparator in v3 Tables A.4 and A.5, using published reference scores. The existing REINVENT, FragGFN, Soft Q-learning, and SyntheMol comparisons are retained. Extending existing comparators to KRAS does not itself introduce new baseline methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a 10,000-oracle-call evaluation using AUC of top-10 scores, top-10 rediscovery evaluation, and top-100 optimization comparisons. These are additional protocols, distinct from v2's retained sampled-molecule comparisons and larger training budgets. The ChEMBL-derived vocabulary experiment also introduces a control for differences in available molecular building blocks.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether novelty persists with ChEMBL-derived building blocks, whether known actives can be rediscovered, and how fingerprint selection affects molecular structural diversity across library sizes. These address substantive questions beyond the previous analyses. The backward-policy and entropy ablation is retained as Figure A.6, having appeared as Figure A.3 in v2.

E5.justification: The new sample-efficiency evaluation reports means and standard deviations over five independent runs; rediscovery reports mean and standard deviation over three seeded models. Existing three-seed standard-error reporting and the eight-seed backward-policy analysis remain. This adds statistical reporting for new protocols, without establishing increased replication of retained experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds rediscovery rewards of 0.90 and 0.48, KRAS results, SynNet comparisons, ChEMBL-vocabulary results, and sample-efficiency scores. Table A.5 reports SynFlowNet AUC above FragGFN but below REINVENT and SynNet on both tasks. Original entries in Table A.2 and the backward-policy table, renumbered from Table 1 to Table 2, remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The GFlowNet definitions, mathematical reasoning, and forward/backward training objectives are unchanged; neither version supplies new proofs relative to the other. Added Equation 4 documents normalization of the already-used docking reward, rather than extending the theoretical analysis.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the backward-policy contribution: v2 claims improved sample quality and diversity, while v3 claims correction of backward trajectories while retaining diverse, high-reward discovery. The abstract's central synthesis-aware generation claim and the conclusion otherwise retain their substantive scope.

C2.justification: New Appendix B.2 explicitly discusses linear synthesis paths, the two-reactant restriction, unmodeled selectivity, reaction conditions, stereochemistry, and inaccessible chemical regions. v3 also interprets rediscovery through chemical-space membership and proposes an explanation for FragGFN's lower rewards. Conversely, it removes v2's caveat about AiZynthFinder using a different reaction library.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 now specifies scaling-experiment budgets, batch size, evaluation samples, validity filtering, H100 hardware, and timing boundaries. Additional documentation covers docking reward penalties and normalization, reaction encoding, and ChEMBL building-block extraction. These materially expand reproducibility information without proving retained experiments were rerun. Table A.1 removes max_nodes=9; the source-code address is merely relocated.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly connects fingerprint action selection to prior large-action-space reinforcement learning and expands the comparison with SynNet. It adds references supporting new evaluations while removing the TACO-GFN discussion and several diffusion-model references. The main research positioning remains intact; duplicated or differently dated citations to the same works are not new research coverage.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include local wording corrections, shortened related work, moving the data description into Appendix A.2, and adding focused rediscovery, sample-efficiency, and outlook subsections. The publication header changes to ICLR 2025. This is a targeted expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the result displays with four new tables and figures for structural diversity and ChEMBL-controlled novelty. Figure 1 is redrawn with clearer flow directions and reaction-encoding information, and Table A.2 gains a row. The synthesis example moves from main-text Figure 3 to Appendix Figure A.3; several other figures are relocated or reformatted.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens scrutiny of central claims: the ChEMBL-vocabulary control addresses a confound in the novelty comparison, budget-limited evaluations clarify practical competitiveness, and the new outlook qualifies real-world synthesizability. These address important validation and interpretation gaps in v2. Incorrect cross-references and Equation 4's inconsistency with its stated normalization range remain reporting defects, but are outweighed by stronger controls, broader evidence, and clearer applicability limits.
